title: The Air Pocket
passages:
Dey had the name in his mouth and nothing behind it.

"Ivo Salas," he said, agreeable, the way a man hands over a tool he's been asked to hold. Behind his teeth Wren's voice came through the bone of his jaw, thin and flat, the way her voice always arrived down here, less a sound than a pressure: *Dey. Say something to her that's yours.*

"Where is he." Nia hadn't let go of the crank. She was maybe fourteen, in a man's coat cut down to her, and her right hand was locked around a wooden grip worn pale and smooth as a tooth. Bolted to the side of the white enamel chest was a spring cell — wind the crank, store the tension, let it unwind slow to keep the inside cold — and the gauge on it sat in the last quarter of its arc. "He said Tuesday. He said he'd bring a winch and a man with a boat and take us up. Where is he."

"He lent me air," Dey said.

He lifted the pony bottle on his chest rig, a stubby aluminum thing the size of a thermos with S.S. scratched into the shoulder, and turned it so her lamp caught the scratches. His exhaust ticked. That was the scrubber's relief valve letting go each time he breathed out — the rebreather stripped the carbon dioxide out of his air with a canister of sodalime and gave the rest back, so every breath he took down here was a breath somebody else had already used. The mouthpiece tasted of another man's spit. He'd been grateful for it for an hour and now he couldn't have said why.

"He gave me this at forty-two meters and told me to keep going down," Dey said. "So I did."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the whole answer I've got."

Nia's jaw worked. "He had a beard. Bad knee, he sat down on the stair to rest it. He put my brother in that box and swore on his mother he'd come back with a ride." She tipped her head at the chest without taking her eyes off Dey. Under the fogged glass of the inner lid a small boy lay in a nest of foil blankets with a mask over his face, and the fog bloomed and thinned, bloomed and thinned. "So don't stand in my ward breathing his air and tell me his name like it's a coin you found."

*Rude,* Wren said in his jaw. *And correct. Dey, back off the chest, two meters, hands where she can see them.*

"Copy," Dey said, and took a step toward her.

He watched himself do it. That was the part he'd have told her if he'd had the words: he could see his own boot going forward on the tile, and he agreed with it, and the agreement had nothing to do with him. He was warm. That was wrong too. Fifty-two meters down, in a ward with a ceiling of standing water and a curtain rail furred with silt, he was warm as a kitchen, and calm, and it would have taken a better man than Dey Okafor to be frightened on purpose.

Nia saw it. He watched her see it — her eyes going to his, then to the lamp, then back, checking whether he was tracking, and not liking the answer. She'd seen the deep do this. He could tell by the way she stopped arguing and started measuring.

"Say my name," she said.

"You haven't given it."

"Say his."

Dey reached for the man and got a shape with the middle missing. A cough, wet at the bottom of it. A hand pushing a bottle across something. A voice saying *keep going down*, which was the only sentence that had survived, and it had come loose from whoever said it.

"Ivo Salas," he said, warm and helpful, holding out the borrowed bottle. "He's a friend of yours?"

Nia's hand stayed on the crank. Her other one went flat against the glass over her brother's mask, and she said, very quietly, "Oh, you're *gone*."

The tick stopped.

Not slowed — stopped. For an hour the scrubber's relief valve had been letting go in Dey's exhaust, a dry little *tick* every time he breathed out, keeping time in the hinge of Wren's jaw like a clock in the next room. Now the room was quiet. The tether stood stiff over the helipad rail, the wind came off the water in long cold shoves, and down the bone line there was nothing at all. No tick. No breath to make one.

"Dey." She had the slate open on her knee — the recorder that logged everything a diver saw and did — and its screen showed the flat green line of a man not breathing. Four years she'd worked from the other side of that line. A diver came up hollow, missing an hour, and she took his slate home and built the hour back for him, cleaned it up, spliced the parts that would gut him out at the seam so what he heard was true but survivable. She was good at it. She had never once done it live. "Dey, breathe in on my mark. In—"

Nothing.

"You are not doing this to me on a Tuesday," she said. "In. Now."

Down in the ward Nia's hand was flat against the glass and Dey was watching her, warm and agreeable, a man watching weather come in. Wren could see all of it through his own eyes on the feed — the fogged lid, the girl, the gauge in the last quarter of its arc — and she could not reach the part of him that had quit. There was no take to redo. No seam to splice. If he went, he went in the only version there was.

"In," she said, softer, the way you'd talk to something standing on a ledge. "And out. That's all it ever is. You've done it your whole life. In—"

The tick came back. One, small and dry, and the green line lifted and fell.

Wren put her forehead against the cold rail for exactly one second. Then she keyed the boat channel. "Sol. It's not cargo." Her voice came out level, which she'd be proud of later. "The twelve-thousand case is two kids. A girl, maybe fourteen. A boy in the box, small, on a mask. That's the manifest. That's the whole thing the Factor's paying for."

Sol didn't answer. Wren could feel her not answering, the whole boat holding still around it.

"Copy," Sol said finally. Just that.

That was when the drone came down through the hatch.

It dropped out of the standing water overhead without a splash too small to matter — a broker's thing the size of two fists, four rotors and a lens on a little gimbal — and hung in the air a meter above Dey's head. The lens turned down. A voice came out of it, pleasant, the Factor's own, thinned by water and distance: *"Manifest confirms. One sealed cryo unit. Seals intact. Count: one."* The lens ticked as it counted, patient, thorough. *"Value confirmed. Awaiting ascent."*

On the helipad Wren watched Sol watch the tether. The captain's face did nothing at all.

Her thumb came off the brake.

The tether came tight.

Dey felt it in his ribs before he understood it — the harness drawing up under his arms, his boots skating a hand's width across the tile, the slack going out of the line with a sound like a rope taking weight. Topside, a thumb had come off a brake. He got a fist through the chest's folding handle and held, and the line held him, and for a moment the two of them argued through his ribs.

"Wren. Tell her hold."

"Sol, hold — hold, he's got the case—" A pause the length of a bad decision. Then the pull quit, and the drone's lens ticked on overhead, counting nothing, patient as a gull.

*Two minutes,* Wren said in his jaw. *I bought you two. What am I looking at?*

"White enamel box," Dey said. "Feet welded to the deck so it doesn't slide. Glass port in the lid."

*Is it the Factor's?*

"Ask the girl."

Nia hadn't taken her hand off the crank. "You're not carrying it up."

"No," Dey said, and meant it, and that was the strangest thing in the whole strange hour: he could still mean things.

"Then look at it and go." She jerked her chin at the lid. "Med chest. Hospital issue. You put a live culture in a cold box, it keeps. You take it out, it dies. Four degrees, no higher, or my brother's medicine turns to soup in an afternoon."

*Cold chain,* Wren said, mostly to herself, the way she did when a thing stopped being a rumor. *Dey, her spring gauge. Read me the number.*

"Quarter arc," he said. "Last quarter."

"And the cell's dead. Died last March." Nia's voice went flat and quick, a report she'd given to nobody for a year. "So I wind it. Forty turns to the mark, holds four hours, I do it in my sleep. Two hundred and forty turns a day, three hundred sixty days. Don't tell me about boats. A man with a boat came in April, said four hundred for the both of us, then he saw the box and stopped talking about us altogether."

*Twenty-two years,* Wren said.

"What?"

*Nothing. Fatigue in that spring is wrong for a year, that's all. Keep her talking.*

"So it's medicine," Dey said.

"It's nine doses and a boy who needs one every other day." Nia's chin came up. "You want to know what happens if your drone's boss gets it? It goes on a shelf in a tower on the high ground with a compressor humming and a card on it that says what it cost, and Teo gets eighteen days. Eighteen. Now leave."

The fog on the inner glass stopped blooming.

It had been going in and out since Dey came through the hatch, bloom and thin, bloom and thin, and now it just sat there, gray, a smear with a shape behind it. Dey saw it in his own eyes and knew what it meant, and Nia saw him know, and she was already turning, and she was already too slow because her left hand was on the crank and it would not come off the crank.

"Get the port," she said.

He had it open before she finished. Cold came up out of the box, honest cold, the first cold he'd felt in an hour, and inside on a foam bed there was a rack of glass ampoules with numbers inked on them, and he took the one she pointed at with her whole shaking arm. She got the boy's mask off one-handed and the dosing line in her teeth. Her hands were fast. They were also one pair of hands doing two people's work, and half the dose went across the boy's cheek.

"Hold his jaw," she said. "Hold it *up*."

Dey held it. His hands were very steady. He noticed that the way you notice weather.

Teo coughed — a wet, small, furious sound, a sound with an argument in it — and the fog came back, bloom and thin, and Nia made a noise Dey would have described, if he'd had the word for it, as a woman putting down something heavy.

Then she looked at the gauge and shut the port.

"Forty turns," she said. "I've got to make forty turns up. Opening it costs me cold." She wiped her brother's face with her thumb. "And that was one of nine."

Overhead the drone's lens retracted and extended, satisfied.

*"Count: one,"* it said. *"Seals intact. Awaiting ascent."*

The tick kept time. Wren counted it without meaning to, the way you count anything in a room you can't leave.

"Dey. Boat's name."

"The *Marrow*."

"Captain."

"Sol Ferreira." He considered it, pleasant as a man reading a label. "She writes her trim on the back of her hand in grease pencil and then can't read her own numbers. I don't know why that came out."

"Because it's true, and because you aren't scared of her, which is the best news I've had all morning." Keys going. "I'm getting all of it. Every word onto the slate."

"Where's up?"

He looked at the hatch. Standing water, the pale smear of the topside lamp, and past that nothing he had a word for. "There's water in it."

"Not the hatch. The boat. Which way's the boat."

"I can tell you her engine. Diesel, rebuilt twice, smells like hot oil and other people's washing." He turned the pony bottle slowly in his free hand, the scratches up. "I've lost which hand works the winch. It was in my hands this morning. It isn't in my hands now."

Sol's voice came down the line, flat. "Wren. Clock."

"Ninety seconds."

"You've got ninety."

"I need the two back."

"No."

"Sol—"

"He's on a contract and the season's inside nine hours." Not cruel. Tired, which was worse. "Ninety."

Wren keyed off and put her mouth close to the slate. "Dey. The girl's voice. Stay on it."

"Past fifty," Nia said.

She hadn't come off the crank. Her eyes went over him the way you check a knot you don't trust, and then went lower, to his hands, which were very steady, and then back up.

"I've watched the deep do this. A diver came in April, sat down on the stair at forty-two for two hours because of his knee, and he came up polite as a priest and couldn't tell me one thing he wanted. Not one thing." Her mouth twisted. "It makes you polite. Nobody's home to be rude."

*She's not wrong,* Wren said in his jaw. *Dey, stay with her.*

The gauge sat in the last quarter of its arc. Nia's right hand was locked on the grip, worn pale as a tooth, and it had started to shake — small, fast, a wire in wind. Her lips were the wrong color. She had the look of somebody who'd been eating once every three days and calling it a plan.

"Forty turns to the mark," she said. "Four hours of cold. I can't make forty one-handed and hold my brother's jaw."

Then she did the thing she hadn't done in a year. She pried her left hand off the glass, took Dey by the wrist — her fingers were cold as the box — folded his hand around the crank, and kept her own hand over the top of his.

"Turn," she said. "Slow still counts. I'll count."

He turned. The cell took the tension with a sound like a ratchet in a wall, and overhead the drone's lens ticked along with it, patient, thorough.

"Ten. Keep going."

"My hands are steady."

"Yeah." She didn't look up. "I noticed."

Twenty-two turns in she said it fast, the way you rip tape, because slow would have been impossible. "When you go up, we go up. Both of us and the box. I'll wind it on the way, I'll wind it in your boat, I'll wind it in the rain. I'll pay the four hundred. I'll pay twelve."

"Thirty," said Dey.

"Thirty-one." Her voice cracked and she kept going anyway. "Don't be the man from April. He talked about us fine until he saw the box."

On the helipad the wind shoved the tether and Wren said nothing at all, because there was nothing on the boat channel she was willing to say out loud.

"Ivo Salas put my brother in that box." Nia's chin came up. "He swore on his mother he'd come back with a winch and a man with a boat. He said Tuesday."

Her hand stopped the crank at thirty.

"It's Tuesday," she said. "So where is he?"
